source.title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether independently fine-tuned models share causally relevant components and whether activations at shared components have comparable effects, using head tracing, replacement, and transfer rather than a model-scale representation-similarity measure.
record.gate_note: The study reports new results on shared attention-head locations, their interventions, and cross-organism activation transfer. Cited results about prior representational convergence are not recorded. Layer scans and steering results used to select the tracing anchor are selection diagnostics, not results about convergence. General EM rates, the benign-control pilot, and the mathematics check do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study looks at component overlap and cross-model activation transfer in a new setting: three emergent-misalignment LoRA fine-tunes of one base model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct). The comparison of independently traced head sets and the cross-organism transplants bear on V5 (recurring components) and V4 (interchangeability). The overlap check also touches V7, which says convergence stays incomplete. This is not the original methods' setting, so T3 fits better than T2. All organisms share frozen base weights, so recurrence at identical head coordinates is partly expected by construction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that EM fine-tunes share causally relevant attention-head locations and that these heads are partially functionally interchangeable on fixed-response preference within a common architecture. They explicitly do not claim circuit completeness or minimality, recurrence across architectures or independent seeds, or equivalence in free generation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses direction-based activation tracing, causal head replacement, and cross-organism activation transfer to test component overlap and function; it does not use a scale sweep or direct pairwise representation-distance comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The tracing anchor was fixed at layer 23 for all organisms. The study notes that head-level patching and its evaluation metric/intervention scheme may affect circuit identification, but does not experimentally compare alternative metrics or settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing each organism's own five traced heads with Base contributions cuts judged EM (e.g. finance 50.7%→12.5%), more than layer-matched random sets, without lowering coherence. Zero-ablation and restoration diagnostics agree.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment in LoRA fine-tunes is partly localized to a small set of attention heads whose replacement reduces EM.

record.problems: Only three fine-tunes of one base architecture are tested; independent initialization seeds and new architectures are not tested. Fixed response pairs were generated by the medical organism, which the authors say may introduce distributional bias. Cross-organism transfer is evaluated on nine test-labelled response pairs (with eight eligible for two targets) and fixed-response preference, not free-generation equivalence. The authors state that head-level patching does not establish circuit completeness or minimality and does not isolate the specific parameter updates responsible for EM.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the claim versions tested. General EM rates, tracing-anchor layer scans, steering diagnostics, the benign-control pilot, and the mathematics check were left out because they do not measure convergence or cross-organism interchangeability.

untested.parts: No size or capability sweep, and no cross-architecture, cross-objective or cross-data comparison.
No different-initialization runs. The organisms share frozen base weights and differ only in LoRA data; the authors list independent seeds as untested.

Untested: linear maps, stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, cross-architecture mapping, and transfer during free generation. Only identity transplant at three heads on fixed teacher-forced responses was tested.
Untested: recurrence across architectures or independently pretrained models, and SAE features or neurons. Complete circuits were not established.
No comparison of metrics, settings or out-of-distribution inputs. A single tracing layer and a single ranking metric were used.
No test of whether the shared base or shared fine-tuning recipe causes the overlap, and no test of plateauing.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2 is changed to T3, because this is a new setting (EM LoRA fine-tunes) rather than an alternative method for the original question. The key caveat is that all organisms share frozen base weights and differ only in low-rank adapters. Identical head coordinates and identity-map transplants are therefore much weaker evidence of convergence than comparisons of independently trained models. Per-organism intervention rows (r8–r22) concern EM localization, not convergence, and are relinked to none. The 'reversed' states on random controls r15–r16 were wrong. Self-transplant rows are sanity checks. Transfer effect sizes are small in absolute margin (~0.06–0.12) and use 8–9 prompts generated by the medical organism. The V7 label rests only on the incompleteness of overlap; the cause part of V7 is untested.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, and no comparison of representations across models with different architectures, objectives, or pretraining data.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.

The organisms are independently fine-tuned on different domains from a common base; the study does not compare different initialization seeds or test shared features/subspaces across seed-trained networks.

Tests transplanting activations at three shared head locations and their effect on fixed-response preference. It does not test linear maps, stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mapping, or equivalence during free generation.

Tests recurrence and functional effects of attention-head locations, not recurrence of interpretable neurons, SAE features, or other circuits; only one base architecture and three domain fine-tunes are studied.
No comparison of similarity metrics, metric settings, neighbour counts, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.

The study reports partial head overlap and notes shared-architecture and response-dataset limitations, but does not test whether shared training data/objectives cause the overlap, compare against a common-reality explanation, or test whether alignment plateaus.
